title: Which dice colourings make the number of colours seen most uncertain? Fair coins, hub designs and a local limit theorem for doubly stochastic occupancy
shortTitle: Most uncertain dice colourings: share one colour
oneLine: To make the number of colours seen on rolled coins most uncertain, put one colour on every coin; for dice of any size, unbalanced hub designs beat every evenly spread design.
abstract: Paint the faces of m dice with n colours, never repeating a colour on one die, roll them all and count the distinct colours that appear. Pelekis asked which painting makes this count most uncertain, in the sense of largest Shannon entropy. He proved an upper bound of order half the logarithm of n and conjectured that the colours should be spread as evenly as possible, that the cycle and circular designs are optimal, and (his Conjecture 4.1) that the circular design has entropy at least ½log₂(n/r) − O(1). Research records of the trureturing project refuted the even-spread and circular conjectures at one small size each. This candidate settles the coin case: for every sufficiently large palette and every number of coins m ≥ n, the unique optimum is a star, with one colour on every coin paired once with each other colour; up to three extra coins duplicate distinct pairs, and four or more all duplicate one pair. The palette threshold is not explicit; it is at least ten, by an exactly certified nine-colour exception. Three colours are solved for every number of coins. For every number of faces r ≥ 2, with as many dice as colours, explicit unbalanced hub designs beat every evenly spread design by at least ½log 1.5 nats once n is large, so the even-spread conjecture and circular maximality fail for every r; for 2- to 8-sided dice this is certified exactly up to 120 colours. Conjecture 4.1 is proved with an absolute constant. The tool is a local limit theorem for the number of distinct values when each row of a doubly stochastic matrix is sampled once, with all errors controlled by twice the expected number of colliding pairs: the optimal local rate, every fixed order of the lattice Edgeworth expansion, the squared-skewness entropy correction and a saddlepoint formula. The central limit theorem in this setting is due to D'yakonova and Mikhailov. Limits: the coin threshold is ineffective, and the optimum for dice with three or more faces is not identified. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem A, Theorems 9.1 and 9.3 (proof, main): there is an absolute n₀ such that for n ≥ n₀ and m ≥ n coins the unique entropy maximiser is the star: one colour on every coin, paired once with each other colour; t = m − n + 1 extra coins go on t distinct spokes if t ≤ 3 and all on one spoke if t ≥ 4. n₀ is not explicit; n₀ ≥ 10 by an exact nine-colour certificate. Three colours are solved for every m.

Theorem B and Corollary 7.4 (proof, exact certificates): for every r ≥ 2 and m = n, hub designs beat every evenly spread design by at least ½log 1.5 − o(1) nats, so Pelekis's even-spread conjecture and cycle and circular maximality fail for every r and all large n; certified for 2 ≤ r ≤ 8 from n = 6, 10, 16, 20, 26, 31, 38 up to 120.
Corollary 1.1 (proof): every r-regular design has entropy ½log₂ n + O(1) bits with an absolute constant, which proves Pelekis's Conjecture 4.1.

Theorem C (proof): for every doubly stochastic matrix, cS ≤ σ² ≤ S/2, a local limit theorem with optimal error C/√S, every fixed order of the lattice Edgeworth expansion, H = ½log(2πeσ²) − κ₃²/(12σ⁶) + O(S⁻²) and a saddlepoint formula; the central limit theorem is D'yakonova and Mikhailov's.
Theorem 6.2 (proof): the eventual entropy maximisers among regular designs of ranks two and three.

narration:
Imagine painting a handful of coins, or dice, with colours. Each die carries different colours on its faces, but a colour can appear on many dice. Now roll everything and count how many different colours show up. How should you paint the dice so that this count is as unpredictable as possible?

The mathematician Christos Pelekis asked this question. He proved an upper limit on the uncertainty, and he guessed that the colours should be spread as evenly as possible, with a simple ring-shaped design as the winner. An online research project later found small cases where those guesses fail.

This release shows that the opposite strategy wins. For coins, once there are enough colours, the single best painting puts one shared colour on every coin and pairs it once with each of the other colours. Any leftover coins repeat a few different pairs when there are at most three of them, and otherwise they should all repeat the same pair. The shared colour is almost certain to appear, so the uncertainty is carried by the other colours, which behave like independent fair coin tosses. The number of colours needed for this is not known exactly. It is at least ten, because a case with nine colours breaks the rule. With three colours, the answer is found for every number of coins.

For dice with more faces, designs in which a few shared colours sit on every die beat every evenly spread design by a fixed margin, so the even-spread and ring guesses fail for every size of die. Exact computer checks confirm this for dice with up to eight faces, across a wide range of palette sizes. The best design for those dice is still unknown.

Behind these results is a precise bell-curve law for counts of distinct values, built from hidden fair switches inside the random rolls.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and computer checks rather than by outside peer review, and its full proofs, programs and limits are open for anyone to examine and reuse.
